title: Starship Finally Reaches Orbit: What Flight 14 Proved, and What It Didn't
dek: SpaceX's giant rocket made it to Earth orbit for the first time on September 28, 2026, deployed a batch of next-generation satellites, then cut its mission short.
body: For years, Starship test flights have followed suborbital paths, arcing most of the way around the planet before coming down in the ocean. On September 28, 2026, that changed. SpaceX's 14th Starship test flight lifted off from Starbase in Boca Chica, Texas, and reached Earth orbit for the first time.

Once in orbit, the upper stage released 26 of SpaceX's next-generation Starlink V3 satellites, a real payload rather than the dummy hardware used on earlier tests. That matters: Starship's whole business case rests on carrying heavy, useful cargo to orbit cheaply.

The flight did not go entirely to plan. The mission had been scheduled to last roughly ten hours, but SpaceX ended it after about three, following an earlier engine issue. Starship came down in the Pacific north of Hawaii, then tipped over and burst into flames at the surface, which is how these ocean splashdowns typically end.
Why reaching orbit is such a big step

A suborbital hop can test engines, heat shields and re-entry. Orbit is a different game. A vehicle in orbit has to prove it can relight its engines reliably to come home, because there is no ballistic path that brings it back on its own. That is exactly the capability a cut-short mission leaves partly unproven, and it is the one regulators and future crews will care most about.

Starship is meant to eventually carry crew and cargo to Earth orbit, the Moon and Mars. Every flight now is less about spectacle and more about data: how the engines behave over long coasts, how the heat shield survives repeated use, and how quickly the next vehicle can fly.

The headline is 'first orbit,' but the real test is the next one. A rocket that can reach orbit, do a full-length mission, and land on schedule again and again is what changes spaceflight economics. Flight 14 moved the needle; Flight 15 has to show it wasn't a one-off.
credit: Flight conducted by SpaceX. Reporting from ABC News, LiveNOW from FOX and OneIndia.

title: From Simulation to the Real World: Robotics' Big 2026 Conference Season
dek: IROS 2026 just wrapped in Pittsburgh with nearly 5,000 submissions, and the dominant theme of the year is teaching robots in virtual worlds so they work in ours.
body: Robotics research runs on two flagship conferences. ICRA 2026 took place in Vienna from June 1 to 5. IROS 2026, the other giant, ran in Pittsburgh from September 27 to October 1. The scale tells its own story: IROS received 4,947 paper submissions this year and accepted 1,585 of them, an acceptance rate of about 36%.
The theme of the year: sim-to-real

Training a robot in the physical world is slow, expensive and occasionally destructive. Training it in simulation is fast and cheap, but robots trained that way often fail when they meet real friction, lighting and clutter. Closing that 'sim-to-real gap' is one of the field's central problems.

At ICRA 2026, NVIDIA's research teams presented eight robotics papers aimed squarely at that gap. They covered coordinating several robot arms at once, navigation that adapts across different kinds of robots (a framework called COMPASS), precision grasping, and complex assembly tasks.

NVIDIA has said it plans to release its next-generation GR00T N2 robotics models by the end of 2026, aimed at stronger reasoning and learning from multiple kinds of input. Industrial partners such as ABB and KUKA are part of that ecosystem, which suggests these research ideas are heading toward factory floors, not just lab demos.

The most interesting shift isn't any single robot. It's that the bottleneck is moving from hardware to data. Whoever can generate the most realistic practice for robots, cheaply, wins. Watch for open simulation tools and shared datasets; they will decide who can compete.
credit: Research by NVIDIA Research and the IROS / ICRA author communities. Conference figures from OMRON SINIC X.

title: Precision Gene Editing Gets Sharper, and the Ethics Debate Gets Louder
dek: Base editing in human embryos, AI-designed CRISPR proteins, and a renewed argument about where the line should be.
body: Classic CRISPR works like molecular scissors: it cuts DNA and lets the cell repair the break, which can introduce errors. Newer tools are far more precise. Base editing, for example, changes a single DNA letter without cutting both strands. In 2026, these precision tools moved into some of the most sensitive territory in biology.

In June 2026, Cambridge researchers reported in Nature that they had, for the first time, used base editing to study gene function in human embryos, revealing the role of a master gene in early development. The goal is understanding, not pregnancy: knowing which genes steer the first days of development could eventually help explain infertility and early miscarriage.

Around the same time, US scientists at Columbia University reported editing early human embryos, not intended for pregnancy, with unprecedented accuracy. Scientific American noted that the work revived worries about future uses, eight years after the gene-edited babies scandal in China.
AI starts designing the editors themselves

A study from Nobel laureate Jennifer Doudna's team, published in Science, described RNA-guided DNA-cutting enzymes designed with artificial intelligence. Their sequences differ substantially from anything found in nature, yet they match or beat natural versions in activity and bring new properties. It is an early sign that the toolkit for editing life is no longer limited to what evolution happened to produce.

Two trends are converging: editing is getting precise enough to study human development directly, and AI is generating new editing tools faster than we can catalogue them. That is great for medicine and a real test for oversight. The public conversation needs to keep pace with the lab.
credit: Research by teams at the University of Cambridge, Columbia University, and Jennifer Doudna's lab. Coverage via Scientific American and Science Media Centre Spain.

title: A Drone Planner That Promises Not to Crash, Even Around Things It Has Never Seen
dek: MIT engineers built SANDO, a flight planner that keeps drones clear of moving obstacles in unmapped spaces by reasoning only about how fast those obstacles could possibly travel.
body: Flying a drone through an empty room is easy. Flying it through a collapsed building, a mine tunnel or a busy warehouse is not, because the robot has no map in advance and some of the obstacles are moving. Most planning software handles this in one of two ways: it assumes the world holds still, or it dodges moving things on a best-effort basis with no real promise that it will succeed. A team at MIT has published a planner that aims to close that gap with a formal safety guarantee.

The system is called SANDO, short for Safe AutoNomous trajectory planning for Dynamic unknOwn environments. It was developed by Kota Kondo, who recently completed his PhD in aeronautics and astronautics at MIT, together with Jesús Tordesillas of Comillas Pontifical University in Madrid, MIT graduate students Juan Rached, Lili Sun and Yixuan Jia, and senior author Jonathan How, who leads MIT's Aerospace Controls Laboratory. The work appears in IEEE Transactions on Robotics, and MIT announced it on October 7.

The key idea is that the planner does not try to predict exactly where a moving obstacle will go. It only needs an upper limit on how fast that obstacle can travel. As Kondo put it to MIT News, the planner only needs "the top speed the obstacles could reach." From that limit, SANDO draws a sphere around each tracked obstacle that grows over time to cover every place it could possibly be.
How it keeps the path clear

Onboard, SANDO detects nearby obstacles, groups them and tracks them. It then builds what the researchers call a safety corridor: a chain of connected 3D regions that are guaranteed to be empty, not just now but at the moments the drone will pass through them. A separate heat-map planner marks crowded areas as hot spots and nudges the route toward quieter space. Inside that corridor, the software computes the fastest trajectory to the goal, and it keeps rebuilding both the corridor and the path as the flight unfolds. The math is simplified enough to run on the drone's own computer, so it can replan quickly.

In simulation, the MIT team reports that SANDO reached its goals faster than several leading planners and avoided collisions in every environment it was tested in. On real hardware, it avoided every moving obstacle across 12 test flights using only onboard sensors and computing. The code has been released publicly on GitHub.

The guarantee is only as good as its assumption. If something moves faster than the speed limit the planner was given, it falls outside the safety bubble, a caveat New Atlas highlighted in its coverage. Twelve flights is also a modest test campaign. According to New Atlas, the team's next steps include reducing the computing load, connecting the planner to AI tools that accept plain-language instructions, and coordinating several drones at once. The research was funded in part by Singapore's Defense Science and Technology Agency.

What I like here is the shift from "usually avoids crashes" to a stated guarantee with clearly stated conditions. That is the kind of claim engineers and regulators can actually reason about. For search-and-rescue and inspection drones, I would watch how well the speed-limit assumption holds up around unpredictable things like people and debris, and whether the approach scales to swarms.
credit: Research by Kota Kondo, Juan Rached, Lili Sun, Yixuan Jia and Jonathan P. How (MIT Aerospace Controls Laboratory and LIDS) with Jesús Tordesillas (Comillas Pontifical University). Coverage via MIT News and New Atlas.
sources: MIT News: Planning system ensures a robot's flight path will remain collision-free

title: Perseverance Becomes the Farthest-Driving Vehicle on Another World
dek: NASA's Perseverance rover has passed Opportunity's long-standing record for distance driven beyond Earth, largely by doing its own navigating across the Martian terrain.
body: For more than a decade, the record for the longest drive on any world other than Earth belonged to Opportunity, the hardy NASA rover that roamed Mars from 2004 to 2018. That record has now fallen. On October 11, 2026, the mission's 2,006th Martian day, NASA's Perseverance rover pushed its odometer to 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), edging past Opportunity's 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers). NASA announced the milestone on October 12.
A record set in a fraction of the time

The striking part is not the small margin but the pace. Perseverance covered its distance in about five and a half years, while Opportunity needed almost 15 to build its total. Earlier in the mission, Perseverance had already passed the best distances ever driven on the Moon: the Soviet Lunokhod 2 rover's 24.2 miles (39 kilometers) in 1973 and the 22.2 miles (35.7 kilometers) covered by Apollo 17's astronauts in their lunar rover in 1972.

Steven Lee, who manages the Curiosity and Perseverance missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, noted that the original mission plan called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving. The rover has more than doubled that, and the team expects the total to keep growing.

The main reason for the speed is autonomy. Perseverance uses a self-driving system called AutoNav. Engineers on Earth choose waypoints, and the rover fills in the route on its own: it photographs the ground as it rolls, builds a 3D map of hazards such as rocks and slopes, and steers around them without waiting for instructions. The team describes this as thinking while driving. On a good day the rover can cover up to 412 meters (1,351 feet).

According to NASA, more than 90 percent of Perseverance's total distance was driven under AutoNav, compared with about 5 percent for Opportunity and its twin, Spirit. The rover processes about 600,000 measurement points each time it surveys the terrain ahead. Mark Maimone, deputy team chief for robotic operations, said newer software has made the rover a better driver than it was at landing, letting it steer less and roll more.

The milestone arrives as Perseverance starts its first mission extension, approved by NASA to run from October 2026 to about the end of 2028 and focused on the rim of Jezero Crater. The rover is heading to a site called Idubi in an area nicknamed Lac de Charmes, just west of the rim, where scientists hope very old rocks preserve traces of ancient hot-water systems. After that it will travel south along the rim toward Rainbow Falls, a block of ancient crust about 100 meters wide that was pushed up by the impact that carved the crater. So far the rover has collected 29 rock and regolith samples. One practical obstacle remains: glare in the navigation cameras still forces it to stop by mid-afternoon when it is driving toward the Sun.

The headline is a distance record, but the real story is software. Opportunity was mostly driven step by step from Earth; Perseverance does most of its own route finding, and that is why it covered the same ground in roughly a third of the time. For future missions, every hour a rover spends waiting for instructions is an hour of science lost, so autonomy is a multiplier on everything else. Watch how the team handles the camera glare problem and whether these navigation lessons carry over to the next generation of lunar and Martian vehicles.
credit: Research and operations by NASA's Perseverance rover team at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, including project manager Steven Lee and deputy robotic operations chief Mark Maimone. Coverage via NASA Science, EarthSky and Sci.News.

title: Turning Immune Cells Into Cancer Hunters Without Ever Leaving the Body
dek: MIT engineers used targeted lipid nanoparticles to reprogram natural killer cells inside mice, clearing tumors and healing an autoimmune liver disease without any lab-grown cells.
body: Engineered immune cells have become one of medicine's most powerful tools against blood cancers. In CAR T therapy, a patient's T cells are collected, given a cancer-recognizing receptor in a lab, multiplied and infused back. It works, but it is slow, costly and hard to scale. A team at MIT led by chemical engineer Daniel Anderson has now shown, in mice, a way to skip the lab entirely. Their study, published on October 13 in Nature Biotechnology, reprograms a different kind of immune cell, the natural killer (NK) cell, directly inside the body.
A delivery package with an address label

The approach relies on lipid nanoparticles, the same kind of tiny fat bubbles that carried mRNA in COVID-19 vaccines. Here the particles carry mRNA instructions for a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR, the engineered sensor that tells an immune cell which target to attack. To make sure the cargo reaches the right cells, the researchers coated the particles with antibody fragments that latch onto receptors found on NK cells. Once inside, the NK cells read the mRNA and display the CAR.

The CAR can be swapped to aim at different targets. The team built versions that recognize CD19, a marker on B cells, and CD3, a marker on T cells. The work was led by postdoc Yuang Chen and graduate students Julia Monkovic and Haseeb Mughal, with Robert Langer among the co-authors.

According to MIT, about 80 percent of the targeted NK cells were reprogrammed after the particles were infused. In a model of aggressive melanoma, three of five treated mice went into complete remission. In mice given human immune systems and a T cell lymphoma, five injections eradicated the tumors, a result comparable to conventional CAR NK cells made outside the body. In a model of autoimmune hepatitis, where the body's own T cells attack the liver, a single injection destroyed the rogue T cells and the liver damage healed.

That last result points to a key advantage of NK cells. When CAR T cells are aimed at a marker that T cells themselves carry, they can end up attacking one another. NK cells avoid that problem, which makes them a natural fit for diseases driven by T cells. As Chen put it, NK cells can treat "not only T cell cancer, but also T cell autoimmune diseases."
Why it matters, and what is still unknown

No CAR NK therapy has yet been approved by the FDA, partly because manufacturing these cells is so demanding. If an off-the-shelf infusion of nanoparticles could do the job, treatment could become faster and far cheaper. The researchers say they hope to apply the method to autoimmune conditions such as multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis.

Some perspective is needed. Every experiment so far was in mice, some groups were small, and the public summaries do not report long-term durability or detailed safety data. Because mRNA fades over time, how long the reprogrammed cells keep working in people is an open question.

Viraj's perspective: The most interesting shift here is from manufacturing cells to manufacturing a drug. Hospitals already know how to store and infuse a vial of nanoparticles; a personalized cell product needs its own supply chain for every patient. If this holds up, the bottleneck for cell therapy moves from the factory to the chemistry. What I will be watching: safety and dosing data, how long the effect lasts once the mRNA is gone, and whether the autoimmune results carry over to larger animals and, eventually, to a first human trial.
credit: Research by Yuang Chen, Julia Monkovic, Haseeb Mughal, Robert Langer, Daniel Anderson and colleagues at MIT's Department of Chemical Engineering, Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Institute for Medical Engineering and Science. Coverage via MIT News and AZoLifeSciences.

title: One Camera, One Tiny Brain: The AI Drone That Outflew World Champion Pilots
dek: TU Delft's MonoRace drone, steered by a small neural network and a single camera, beat every autonomous rival and three former human world champions at an international race in Abu Dhabi.
body: Drone racing is one of the hardest tests you can set for a flying robot. Pilots thread tiny quadcopters through gates at highway speeds, reacting in fractions of a second. Machines have beaten champion humans before, but only on tracks built for them and with help from outside tracking systems. A team at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands now reports a drone that did it on a course the robot's builders did not control, using only what it carried on board. The study appeared in Science Robotics on October 14.

The system, called MonoRace, comes from TU Delft's Micro Air Vehicle Lab (MAVLab). The paper's authors include Stavrow Bahnam, Robin Ferede, Christophe De Wagter and Guido de Croon, among other members of the group. Their drone has no GPS and no external cameras watching it. It relies on one forward-facing camera and an inertial measurement unit, the same kind of motion sensor found in phones. De Wagter told Popular Science the goal was to see "how much intelligence we could extract from very limited resources."

A neural network reads the camera feed to spot the racing gates, and that estimate is blended with the motion sensor data so the drone knows where it is on the track. A second, very small network then sends commands straight to the four motors about 500 times per second, skipping the usual step of planning a path and then following it. That controller was trained with reinforcement learning, a trial-and-error method, entirely in simulation before it ever flew for real.
How it did in Abu Dhabi

The team entered MonoRace in a 2025 autonomous drone racing competition in Abu Dhabi, flying on a track and hardware supplied by the organizers. According to TU Delft, it reached speeds of up to 100 kilometers per hour (about 62 mph), beat all the other autonomous teams and posted faster runs than three former world champion human pilots. The researchers say it is the first AI-piloted drone to beat human pilots at an international race.

That matters because the best-known earlier result, the University of Zurich's Swift drone in 2022, beat humans on an indoor track it was designed and trained for. As Popular Science noted, Swift's performance suffered when conditions such as lighting changed.

One camera is cheap and light, but at high speed its images become blurry and distorted, which is why the motion sensor is essential. The earlier preprint version of the work is open about other gaps: the drone has no way to avoid other drones, and a collision cost it in a multi-drone race. Its vision system also expects rectangular gates, and some fixes were tuned to this specific track and aircraft. Racing success has not yet carried over to larger robots in messier settings.

Viraj's perspective: The headline is the human win, but the deeper result is how little hardware it took. A single camera, a motion sensor and a network small enough to run on a flight-controller chip is a recipe that could suit inspection, delivery or search drones where weight and cost matter. What I would watch next is whether the Delft group can add obstacle and drone avoidance, and how well the approach generalizes beyond neat rectangular gates.
credit: Research by Stavrow Bahnam, Robin Ferede, Christophe De Wagter, Guido de Croon and colleagues at the Micro Air Vehicle Lab (MAVLab), Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, Delft University of Technology. Coverage via EurekAlert! (TU Delft release) and Popular Science.
sources: EurekAlert! (TU Delft): The science behind the world's fastest autonomous racing drone

title: Orion's Heat Shield Passes Its Crewed Test: NASA's Verdict on Artemis II
dek: Six months after Artemis II splashed down, NASA's engineering analysis finds Orion's heat shield behaved as predicted, with about one-tenth the char damage seen after the uncrewed Artemis I flight.
body: When the uncrewed Artemis I capsule came home from the Moon in 2022, engineers found something they had not expected: chunks of the charred outer layer of Orion's heat shield had broken away. Fixing or working around that problem became one of the biggest questions hanging over Artemis II, the first flight to carry astronauts in Orion. On October 15, NASA published the results of its detailed post-flight engineering analysis, and the answer is reassuring. The shield, the agency says, performed as expected.
What went wrong the first time

Orion's heat shield is built from 186 blocks of Avcoat, an ablative material designed to char and slowly wear away as it absorbs reentry heat. In a December 2024 report, NASA explained that during Artemis I's reentry, gases formed inside the Avcoat could not escape fast enough because the material was not permeable enough. Pressure built up, the Avcoat cracked, and pieces of char broke off. That investigation drew on samples cut from the shield at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center and arc jet tests at NASA's Ames Research Center that recreated the reentry heating.

Rather than rebuild the Artemis II shield, NASA changed the flight path. Engineers shortened the maximum downrange distance Orion would travel during reentry, which limits how long the shield sits in the temperature range where the Artemis I damage happened.

Artemis II carried four astronauts around the Moon and splashed down off San Diego on April 10, 2026. According to NASA, Orion hit the atmosphere at up to 39 times the speed of sound, outside temperatures topped 4,000°F, and the cabin stayed in the mid-70s. The capsule entered within 192 feet of its target point and landed 0.59 miles from where it was predicted to come down.

The headline number is char loss. NASA counted nine spots on the Artemis II shield, compared with 103 after Artemis I, roughly a tenfold reduction in cracking and missing char. The agency also reports that the seams between Avcoat blocks and the material around bolt fittings behaved consistently across both flights. The backshell, covered in about 1,300 ceramic tiles that protect the windows, vents, thrusters and hatch, showed no signs of overheating. Overall, the measured heating matched what pre-flight analysis and ground tests had predicted.

The work is not finished. The shield moved to Marshall in Huntsville, Alabama, where engineers began cutting samples and taking X-ray scans in August. Laser scans of the surface are being compared with pre-flight measurements to see exactly how much material wore away. NASA says upgrades for Artemis III aim to make the Avcoat blocks uniformly permeable, tackling the root cause rather than just steering around it. Artemis III's heat shield is already attached to its crew module at Kennedy Space Center, and that mission is planned for next year in Earth orbit, ahead of a landing attempt NASA targets for Artemis IV in 2028.

Viraj's perspective: This is a good example of engineering margin earned the careful way. NASA did not claim the material problem was solved; it changed the operating conditions, predicted the outcome, and then checked the prediction against the hardware. A tenfold drop in char loss is encouraging, but the real test is the redesigned, more permeable Avcoat. Watch for the recession data from the laser scans and for how the new blocks perform on Artemis III and the faster lunar returns that follow.
credit: Research and post-flight analysis by NASA engineering teams, including work at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, Ames Research Center and Kennedy Space Center. Coverage via NASA and autoevolution.

title: One Infusion, Longer Nights: Base Editing's First Results in a Rare Sugar Disorder
dek: Beam Therapeutics reported early data from six people with glycogen storage disease type Ia, where a single dose of the base editor BEAM-301 stretched how long patients could safely go without food.
body: For people with glycogen storage disease type Ia, or GSDIa, a night's sleep is a scheduling problem. The disease breaks the liver's ability to release stored sugar into the blood, so blood glucose can crash dangerously within a few hours of the last meal. Many patients take measured doses of uncooked cornstarch around the clock, even overnight. On October 13, Beam Therapeutics, a Massachusetts gene editing company, released the first human data for BEAM-301, a one-time treatment designed to fix the faulty gene directly inside the liver.
Correcting a single letter of DNA

GSDIa is an inherited disorder caused by mutations in the G6PC1 gene, which makes an enzyme called glucose-6-phosphatase. The enzyme handles the last step in turning stored glycogen back into blood sugar. BEAM-301 targets one specific spelling error in this gene, known as R83C, which Beam describes as one of the most common disease-causing variants. People with this variant can slip into hypoglycemia within one to three hours without cornstarch.

The treatment uses base editing, a newer form of gene editing that swaps a single DNA letter for another without cutting both strands of the double helix, as classic CRISPR does. The editing machinery travels to the liver inside lipid nanoparticles, the tiny fat bubbles used in mRNA vaccines, given as one intravenous infusion.

The data come from an open-label Phase 1/2 trial and cover six patients as of a June 26 data cutoff: three who received a 20 milligram dose and three who received 40 milligrams. In the lower-dose group, the median time patients could fast before their blood sugar fell too low rose from 2.9 hours to 4.3 hours by day 36. The two evaluable patients in the higher-dose group, who started at a median of 2.5 hours, both reached the trial's ceiling of at least 15 hours of supervised fasting.

Patients also needed less cornstarch. The higher-dose group cut its prescribed daily amount by 71 percent at day 50 and 92 percent at day 93. The lower-dose group saw reductions of 74 percent at day 128 and 71 percent at day 227, but only 11 percent at day 387, a reminder that durability is still an open question.

Every patient had at least one side effect judged related to the treatment. There were five serious adverse events, including three severe infusion reactions, all of which resolved within two to ten days; Beam says it has since changed the steroid regimen given before infusion. Liver enzyme rises were mild and temporary, and no dose-limiting toxicities or deaths were reported. Updated results will be presented as a poster at the European Society of Gene and Cell Therapy congress in Hamburg on October 28, presented by Rebecca Riba-Wolman of Connecticut Children's.

These are company-reported results from a handful of people, without a control group and not yet peer reviewed. The high-dose cohort had been followed for a median of only 53 days. Still, going from under three hours to the 15-hour maximum would, if it lasts, reshape daily life.

Viraj's perspective: Base editing has long proven itself in dishes and animals. What makes BEAM-301 worth watching is that the readout is something patients feel directly: hours of safe fasting and fewer cornstarch doses. The questions for the Hamburg data and beyond are simple. Does the 40 milligram effect last past a few months, does the lower dose fade as the day 387 figure hints, and can the infusion reactions be tamed? If they break the right way, this could become a template for other single-letter liver diseases.
credit: Research by Beam Therapeutics and the investigators of the BEAM-301 Phase 1/2 trial (NCT06735755), with ESGCT data presented by Rebecca Riba-Wolman, M.D., of Connecticut Children's. Coverage via CRISPR Medicine News and Pharmacally.

title: From One Video to Seven Straight Throws: Google DeepMind's Video-to-Sim-to-Real Demo
dek: Google DeepMind says its new Gemini 4 Argon model watched a person play cornhole, wrote its own physics simulation, and helped Apptronik's Apollo humanoid land seven throws in a row.
body: Teaching a robot a new physical skill usually starts long before the robot moves. Engineers build a virtual copy of the task in a physics simulator, tune it by hand so it behaves like the real world, and then let the robot practice there thousands of times. That modeling step can take weeks. On October 13, Google DeepMind introduced Gemini 4 Argon, its newest frontier AI model, and showed an internal robotics test aimed squarely at that bottleneck.
Watching, then building the practice field

In the demonstration, the team gave Argon a video of a person playing cornhole, the backyard game of tossing beanbags at a slanted board with a hole. According to Google's announcement, the model worked out the spatial layout of the scene from the footage, estimated the whole-body joint movements a robot would need to make the throw, and then wrote the simulation code itself. Coverage of the demo says the practice took place in MuJoCo, a widely used open-source physics engine, where the model reviewed failed attempts and changed its approach, for example adjusting the stance and swing to fit a robot's body rather than a human's.

The result was then moved onto real hardware: Apollo, a humanoid robot built by Apptronik, an Austin, Texas company that works with Google DeepMind. In a real-world trial, Apollo landed seven consecutive throws. Google calls the workflow Video-to-Sim-to-Real and says it shrinks weeks of manual simulation work into a few hours.
Part of a broader model launch

The robotics test was one piece of a larger release. Gemini 4 Argon is a general model available to developers through Google's API, and the company highlighted uses ranging from software engineering to drug discovery and security. On the robotics side, Google reported a score of 87 percent on ERQA, a benchmark of multiple-choice questions about spatial and physical reasoning, which it says beats other frontier models. That number measures how well the model reasons about the physical world in a quiz format, not how well a robot performs tasks.
What the demo does and does not show

This was an internal company test, not a peer-reviewed study, and outside outlets were careful to say so. Google has not published how many total attempts were made, how much human engineering went into the setup, or how the seven-shot streak fits into the overall run; reporting notes the workflow included feedback from where earlier throws landed. Cornhole is also a single, fairly forgiving task. The weeks-to-hours claim comes from Google and has not been independently measured.

Viraj's perspective: The headline is not that a humanoid can toss a beanbag. It is that a general AI model may be able to draft the simulator itself from ordinary video, which is one of the slowest, most expert-heavy steps in robot learning. If that holds up, the supply of robot training scenarios could grow as fast as people can record videos. What I want to see next: a written technical report with attempt counts and failure cases, tests on tasks where physics is less forgiving, like handling soft or fragile objects, and independent labs reproducing the pipeline on their own robots.
credit: Research and demonstration by Google DeepMind, with the Apollo humanoid from Apptronik. Coverage via Humanoids Daily, Humanoid.guide, Crypto Briefing and IEEE Spectrum.

title: Japan's MMX Heads for Phobos to Bring Home a Piece of a Martian Moon
dek: JAXA's Martian Moons eXploration spacecraft lifted off on an H3 rocket and is now bound for Mars, aiming to orbit Phobos, land on it and return at least 10 grams of its surface to Earth in 2031.
body: Mars has two small, lumpy moons, Phobos and Deimos, and nobody is quite sure where they came from. On October 19 at 3:41 p.m. EDT (4:41 a.m. on October 20 in Japan), the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) launched a spacecraft built to settle the question by bringing a piece of Phobos home. The Martian Moons eXploration mission, or MMX, rode an H3 rocket from Tanegashima Space Center. JAXA reports the rocket flew as planned and that the spacecraft separated about 71 minutes after liftoff, entering its intended orbit.
A mystery about where two moons came from

Phobos is only about 22 kilometers across and Deimos about 12. One idea is that they are asteroids that wandered too close to Mars and were captured by its gravity. Another is that they formed from rubble thrown into orbit when something large slammed into the planet. Their neat, circular orbits lined up with the Martian equator lean toward the impact story, but the evidence so far is indirect. NASA's Tom Statler told Space.com the moons "may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars." A sample analyzed in labs on Earth could tell the two scenarios apart, and could also shed light on how water and organic material reached the inner planets.
The plan: orbit, scout, land, return

MMX is due to reach the Mars system in August 2027. It will then settle into a special path that keeps it close to Phobos and spend a long stretch mapping both moons from a distance. Before the main spacecraft touches down, it will release Idefix, a 25 kilogram, four-wheeled rover built jointly by the French space agency CNES and the German Aerospace Center (DLR), which will scout the surface and study its texture and makeup. The spacecraft will then land and collect at least 10 grams of material using two tools: JAXA's coring sampler, which digs deeper, and NASA's pneumatic sampler, built by Honeybee Robotics, which gathers surface grains in seconds. A return capsule is planned to land in Australia in 2031, as Japan's Hayabusa missions did.

It is a broad international effort. NASA supplied the MEGANE gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer, built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, to measure which elements make up Phobos. ESA provided deep space communication equipment and will support the mission through its Estrack ground stations. In all, the spacecraft carries more than a dozen science instruments, including cameras, an infrared spectrometer and a laser altimeter.

Japan has returned asteroid samples twice before, from Itokawa and Ryugu, and NASA's OSIRIS-REx brought back material from Bennu. MMX aims for several firsts: the first spacecraft to orbit Phobos, the first sample from a moon other than our own, and the first return trip from the Mars system. The mission was originally planned for 2024 but slipped because of problems with the new H3 rocket, and Mars launch windows only open about every 26 months, so this successful departure matters.

Viraj's perspective: A clean launch is only the opening move of a five-year journey, and the hard parts, a landing in almost no gravity and a long trip home, are still ahead. What makes MMX worth watching is the payoff: a few grams of Phobos could answer a question that orbital pictures have left open for decades. Keep an eye on the August 2027 arrival, Idefix's first drive across a tiny moon, and whether Mars-orbiting rubble ends up carrying traces of Mars itself.
credit: Research by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) and its Institute of Space and Astronautical Science, with partners NASA, Johns Hopkins APL, Honeybee Robotics, CNES, DLR and ESA. Coverage via Space.com and SpacePolicyOnline.com.

title: Plastics With a Built-In Off Switch: Enzymes Help Compostable Polyesters Break Down in the Deep Sea
dek: A University of Tokyo team mixed plastic-digesting enzymes into compostable polyesters, and some of the films almost completely broke down within months on the seafloor, where ordinary biodegradable plastics barely change.
body: "Biodegradable" on a label usually assumes a helpful setting: a warm compost heap or soil packed with microbes. The ocean, and above all the cold, dark deep sea, is far less cooperative, because the microbes that would chew through a plastic are scarce there. A research group led by Tadahisa Iwata at the University of Tokyo has tried a different approach. Rather than waiting for the environment to supply the right enzymes, they built the enzymes into the plastic. Their results were published in Nature on October 21.
Packing the cleanup crew inside the plastic

The team worked with four compostable polyesters already used in products such as bags and films: PBS, PBSA, PCL and PBAT. During manufacturing they blended in two natural enzymes that cut the ester bonds holding these polymers together, a cutinase and a lipase. The amounts were tiny, as little as 0.1 percent of the material by weight in some tests, with up to 3 percent used in certain deep-sea samples.

According to the university's announcement, the design behaves like a start switch. While the plastic stays dry and in use, the enzymes sit locked inside and almost nothing happens. Once the item ends up in the environment and its surface is scratched or broken, water reaches the enzymes and they begin to digest the material around them. In tensile tests, the enzyme-loaded plastics were about as strong as their enzyme-free versions, with almost no difference at the lowest loading.
From the shoreline to 5,500 meters down

The researchers placed samples in coastal seawater a few meters deep, at a deep-sea site 757 meters down, and on the seafloor at 5,503 meters. Deep samples were placed and recovered using the crewed submersible Shinkai 6500 or the remotely operated vehicle Kaimei. Near the coast, some materials almost completely degraded in roughly a month. At 757 meters, several of the films containing cutinase, made from PBS, PBSA and PCL, almost fully disappeared within about five months.

The university reports that this was 5 to 50 times faster than enzyme-free versions at the coast, and 12 to 80 times faster in the deep sea. Lab tests that measured oxygen consumption by microbes suggested the fragments were being converted into carbon dioxide and biomass, not simply crumbling into smaller pieces.
What the results do not show yet

The gains were uneven. On the deepest seafloor, at 5,503 meters, degradation was only moderate. Some analyses were small: microbial DNA sequencing used one sample per condition, and some microbeads escaped through the sample mesh, so their weight loss could not be measured reliably. The study also did not test long-term storage, shelf life or large-scale manufacturing, which would all matter before such plastics reach store shelves. And faster breakdown at sea does not make littering acceptable; collection and recycling remain the first line of defense.

Viraj's perspective: What I like here is the engineering logic. Instead of hoping the ocean supplies the right microbes, the material carries its own cleanup crew and only switches it on once damaged. The open questions are practical: will the enzymes stay active through months on a warehouse shelf, can the switch avoid triggering in humid use, and can the deepest, coldest sites be handled with better enzymes? If those hold up, built-in enzymes could make labels like marine-degradable mean something real.
credit: Research by Tadahisa Iwata's group at the University of Tokyo with co-authors QiuYuan Huang, Noriko Iida, Noriyuki Isobe, Taizo Kabe, Taku Omura, Manikandan Ilangovan, Satoshi Kimura, Jin Ho Seok, Hidetaka Nomaki and Ken-ichi Kasuya, published in Nature. Coverage via Nature's Research Briefing, Bioengineer.org and Tii Technical Information Institute (reprinting the University of Tokyo announcement).

title: A Soft Robot Arm That Runs on Living Algae and Light
dek: Researchers at Delft University of Technology grew living microalgae on a two-layer hydrogel strip that bends one way when the lights go on and back the other way when they go off, enough to hook a rubber ring and grip a small metal ball underwater.
body: Most robots get their motion from motors, batteries and wires. A team at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands has built a tiny soft gripper that gets its motion from something alive instead: a film of green microalgae. The work, led by Marie-Eve Aubin-Tam with PhD candidate Fan Jiang as first author, was published in Nature Communications on October 22.

The device is a flexible strip about 2 centimeters long and roughly 1 millimeter thick. It is made of two different hydrogel layers, soft water-filled polymers that swell or shrink depending on how acidic their surroundings are. Living cells of the single-celled alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, a common lab organism, grow on its surface.

The trick is that the algae change the chemistry around them as they live. In the light, they photosynthesize, pulling in carbon dioxide to make sugars, and they also absorb nitrogen to build new cell parts. Both processes push the pH inside the hydrogel up. Because the two layers react differently to that shift, one swells more than the other and the strip curls, much like a bimetal strip in an old thermostat. When the light is switched off, the algae burn some of their stored fuel and release carbon dioxide, the pH drops again, and the strip bends back the other way.

To show the motion can do useful work, the team shaped the strips into simple light-controlled grippers. Working underwater, one hooked and lifted a rubber ring, and another grasped a small metal ball. According to TU Delft, the strip starts reversing direction within about 10 seconds of the lights going off; the paper's summary gives an initial response time of 10 to 20 seconds. Reaching the largest bend is far slower, taking up to 18 hours, and the researchers report the movement held up over 10 continuous light-dark cycles.

Aubin-Tam said the aim was to explore what becomes possible when living cells are built into functional materials. The paper is co-authored by Friedrich Hans Kleiner, Roland Kieffer, Djanick de Jong and Jeong-Joo Oh.
What it can and cannot do yet

This is a proof of concept, not a product. The university's announcement does not report how much force the gripper produces, how heavy an object it can hold, or how long the algae keep it working. Ten cycles is a promising start but a long way from the thousands a practical device would need, and an hours-long full stroke rules out anything that has to move quickly. The team suggests the approach could suit gentle handling of delicate objects underwater, light-responsive blinds, or farming devices that turn or reshape themselves as sunlight changes. Because the algae draw their energy from light, the researchers expect such systems to need very little outside power, though that has not yet been measured.

Viraj's perspective: I find this a refreshing twist on actuator design. Instead of carrying its own power source, the material lets a living organism turn ambient light into motion, so the energy budget is set by the sun rather than a battery. The obvious limits are speed and stamina. What I will be watching for is whether follow-up work can show stronger forces, many more cycles, and algae that stay healthy for weeks. If it can, slow but self-sustaining living actuators could find a niche where patience matters more than speed, such as greenhouses, aquariums or long-term underwater sensors.
credit: Research by Fan Jiang, Friedrich Hans Kleiner, Roland Kieffer, Djanick de Jong, Jeong-Joo Oh and Marie-Eve Aubin-Tam at Delft University of Technology, published in Nature Communications. Coverage via EurekAlert! (TU Delft release), Mirage News, Bioengineer.org/Scienmag and Tii Technical Information Institute.

title: Two Landers, One Capsule, 14 Days: NASA's Plan for Artemis III
dek: At an October 23 briefing, NASA laid out how Artemis III will spend about two weeks in Earth orbit in 2027, docking Orion with test versions of both Blue Origin's and SpaceX's lunar landers to clear the way for a Moon landing in 2028.
body: Artemis III was once meant to be the mission that put astronauts back on the Moon. Earlier this year NASA changed course and turned it into a test flight closer to home. On October 23, at a news conference at Kennedy Space Center in Florida, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya and Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons explained in detail what that rehearsal will look like and how it feeds into a crewed landing targeted for 2028.
A busy two weeks in low Earth orbit

According to NASA's mission overview, Artemis III is planned for 2027 and will last about 14 days. Its crew is NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas, plus European Space Agency astronaut Luca Parmitano. The mission needs three heavy-lift rockets: Blue Origin's New Glenn, SpaceX's Starship and NASA's Space Launch System, which carries the crew aboard the Orion capsule.

Blue Origin goes first, placing a test version of its Blue Moon lander in a circular orbit roughly 273 miles up, where it can wait for up to 30 days. Once controllers confirm it is healthy, Orion launches, spends its first couple of days on checkouts, then rendezvouses and docks. The astronauts will then spend about two days inside the lander, checking its cabin, controls and life support.

Later in the mission, SpaceX launches a Starship test vehicle from Florida, timed late because Starship cannot loiter in orbit as long. Orion will dock with a fitting on Starship's nose for up to two hours, but the crew will not go inside. The two dockings use different geometries. Orion can then stay up for as many as five more days of suit, sensor and science tests before splashing down in the Pacific off California.

Earlier in 2026 NASA reworked its contracts so that neither company is locked into a specific landing mission. Both landers take part in Artemis III, and NASA says it will pick which provider flies the first 2028 landing later, with a second landing opportunity to follow. As CBS News reported, Parsons said the agency will wait "as long as possible" before choosing.

The two companies are taking different routes to the Moon. NASA describes SpaceX's plan as launching several tanker Starships to fill an orbiting depot, which then fuels the lander before it pushes Orion toward the Moon. Blue Origin is putting off in-space refueling and will instead stack three transfer stages with its lander to reach an elliptical lunar orbit near the south pole. Either way, NASA requires an uncrewed demonstration before any crew flies, and plans two moonwalks of about two hours each on the first landing.

The schedule is tight. CBS News noted that only the most recent of Starship's 13 test flights reached orbit, and that a launch pad explosion in May grounded New Glenn while a new pad is built, with flights expected to resume around the turn of the year. SpaceX has said its first large-scale orbital refueling demonstration is planned for early 2027. Isaacman himself acknowledged that the effort is extremely hard.

Viraj's perspective: I like that NASA is choosing to practice the hardest new steps, docking a small capsule to two very different landers, in Earth orbit where a quick return home is always possible. The thing I will watch is not the 2027 date itself but the precursors: whether SpaceX's refueling demo and New Glenn's return to flight happen on time. If either slips, Artemis III and the 2028 landing will likely slip with them.
credit: Mission planning and announcements by NASA (Jared Isaacman, Amit Kshatriya, Jeremy Parsons and the Artemis program), with lander development by SpaceX and Blue Origin and crew from NASA and the European Space Agency. Coverage via CBS News (William Harwood), Spectrum News 13 and Space.com.

title: A Personalized mRNA Vaccine Passes Its First Phase 3 Test Against Melanoma
dek: At ESMO 2026, Merck and Moderna reported that adding the individualized mRNA vaccine intismeran to Keytruda after melanoma surgery cut the risk of recurrence or death by 42% in a 1,137-patient Phase 3 trial.
body: Cancer vaccines have a long history of disappointing results. That makes the data presented on October 24 at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress 2026 in Madrid worth paying attention to. In the Presidential Symposium, researchers from the INTerpath-001 trial, led by principal investigator Professor Georgina Long of Melanoma Institute Australia and the University of Sydney, reported Phase 3 results for intismeran autogene, a personalized mRNA vaccine developed by Merck and Moderna. According to the companies, the results have been accepted for publication in The New England Journal of Medicine.
A vaccine built for one patient

Intismeran is not an off-the-shelf shot. Merck describes how each dose starts from the patient's own tumor sample, which is compared against their normal DNA to find the mutations that only the cancer carries. A synthetic mRNA is then made that encodes up to 34 of these tumor-specific markers, called neoantigens. Once injected, the body reads the mRNA and displays the markers to the immune system, training T cells to recognize the cancer if it tries to come back. The vaccine is given alongside pembrolizumab (Keytruda), a checkpoint inhibitor that releases a brake on those same T cells.

The study enrolled 1,137 people whose stage IIB to IV melanoma had been completely removed by surgery, a group at real risk of relapse. Two out of three received the vaccine plus Keytruda, and the rest received a placebo plus Keytruda, for about a year. After a median follow-up of roughly two years, the combination reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 42% (hazard ratio 0.58). At two years, 82.2% of patients on the combination were alive and free of recurrence, compared with 70.0% on Keytruda alone. The risk of the cancer spreading to distant organs, or of death, fell by 38%.

One detail stands out. In the first six months the two groups looked almost identical, and the benefit only appeared afterward, which fits the idea that a personalized immune response takes time to build. Side effects were mostly fever, injection-site pain and fatigue, and serious treatment-related events were about as common in both groups (14.2% versus 13.4%). Overall survival data are not mature yet, though the companies report a favorable trend.

Merck and Moderna say they are talking with regulators about the data. The same vaccine approach is being tested in nine Phase 2 and Phase 3 trials, including three Phase 3 studies in non-small cell lung cancer. Speaking to STAT, ESMO scientific co-chair James Larkin of the Royal Marsden Hospital said the strategy "may be applicable to other types of tumors," while stressing that this is still a principle rather than proven fact.

Viraj's perspective: This feels like a turning point for mRNA beyond vaccines against viruses, because it shows a medicine designed from one person's tumor can work at Phase 3 scale. The questions I will watch are practical ones: how quickly each custom vaccine can be made after surgery, what it will cost, whether overall survival improves, and whether the lung cancer trials repeat the result in a very different tumor.
credit: Research by the INTerpath-001 investigators led by Professor Georgina Long (Melanoma Institute Australia and the University of Sydney), with the trial sponsored and the vaccine developed by Merck and Moderna. Coverage via CancerNetwork, AJMC and STAT.

title: Lab-Grown Muscle Gives Tiny Robots a Real Leap
dek: ETH Zurich engineers designed living muscle tissue and its soft scaffold together on a computer, producing centimeter-scale biohybrid robots that bend far more than earlier versions and can jump, walk, swim and grasp.
body: Living muscle is one of nature's best motors: soft, efficient and able to heal itself. Robotics researchers have tried for years to borrow it by growing muscle cells in the lab and attaching them to small robot bodies. The catch has been that these biohybrid machines usually twitch so weakly that you need a microscope to see them move. A team at ETH Zurich's Soft Robotics Lab, led by Professor Robert Katzschmann with doctoral student Aiste Balciunaite and Mike Y. Michelis as co-lead authors, reports a design approach that makes the motion big enough to see with the naked eye. The study appeared in Nature Communications, and ETH announced it on October 22.

Each actuator pairs skeletal muscle tissue, grown from mouse muscle cells, with a soft, water-rich hydrogel scaffold that stretches and bends a bit like living tissue. Instead of building a scaffold first and then fitting muscle onto it, the team designed both parts at once. A computer simulation decided where to place the tissue, how much to use and how stiff the hydrogel should be, while an algorithm searched for the layout that would make the whole part move the most.

The scaffolds were printed with light using a technique called xolography, which takes about a minute per piece, so the researchers could test a design, feed the results back into the simulation and try again. Fine grooves in the scaffold help the tissue anchor firmly and line up its fibers, so less of each contraction's pull is wasted. Balciunaite said the goal was to design the whole thing from scratch on the computer.

The resulting actuators are about 1.5 centimeters long. According to ETH, they achieve up to 11 times the range of motion of earlier systems that use a comparable amount of muscle. When triggered by an electrical pulse, a single contraction pushes one actuator about 5 millimeters off the bottom of its dish, roughly a third of its own length. A walking version covers 6.2 millimeters per second, which the researchers say is faster for its body size than any walking biohybrid robot reported so far. The team also built versions that swim, move across surfaces and grasp objects, though the announcement does not give performance numbers for those.
Still tied to the lab dish

These robots cannot yet survive outside the lab. The muscle must sit in a nutrient solution to stay alive, and the researchers note that anything larger would need an artificial blood supply to deliver oxygen and nutrients and carry away waste. Grown tissue also varies naturally, so two actuators made the same way will not behave identically, unlike factory-made motors. Next, the team wants to better understand and control how the tissue matures. The ETH coverage does not report contraction forces or how long the actuators keep working.

Viraj's perspective: The interesting move here is treating biology as a design variable instead of a fixed ingredient. By letting simulation decide where the muscle goes and how stiff its scaffold should be, the ETH team turned a weak, hard-to-see twitch into a visible jump, which is the kind of step that makes a field start to feel like engineering. The hard problems are still ahead: keeping tissue alive without a dish, getting consistent behavior from one batch to the next, and measuring real forces and lifetimes. If artificial vascular systems start to work at this scale, I would watch for soft medical or inspection devices that need gentle, self-repairing motion more than raw strength.
credit: Research by Aiste Balciunaite, Mike Y. Michelis, M. Filippi, P. Paniagua, O. Yasa and Robert K. Katzschmann at ETH Zurich's Soft Robotics Lab, published in Nature Communications. Coverage via ETH Zurich News and Robotics & Automation News.

title: Swift Signs Off: NASA's Gamma-Ray Burst Hunter Ends Its Mission After Nearly 22 Years
dek: NASA has ended science operations for the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, which made its last observation on October 20 after drag pulled it too low, leaving behind data that has fed roughly 7,000 scientific papers.
body: On October 23, NASA announced that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has ended its science mission. The spacecraft collected its final observation on October 20, after its orbit had sunk to about 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth. At that height the thin upper atmosphere drags on the satellite enough that its telescopes can no longer hold steady on their targets. NASA expects Swift to fall back into the atmosphere within the next few weeks.
Built for the universe's fastest explosions

Swift launched in November 2004 with a planned two-year primary mission. It kept working for more than ten times that long. Its job was to catch gamma-ray bursts, brief and extremely powerful flashes from distant explosions, and then quickly swing its X-ray, ultraviolet and optical telescopes toward the spot before the fading afterglow disappeared. According to NASA, Swift could point at a new burst in about a minute and could schedule up to 75 separate targets in a single day.

That speed paid off early. In May 2005, Swift caught the afterglow of a burst that lasted just 0.03 seconds, the first short burst ever seen with an afterglow. Only a handful of X-ray particles of light were detected, but they supported the idea that short bursts come from colliding neutron stars. Over its lifetime the observatory recorded more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, studied more than 1,400 supernovae, watched stars being torn apart by black holes, and surveyed the whole sky in X-rays. NASA counts about 7,000 published papers that drew on its data. In 2018 the mission was renamed for Neil Gehrels, its first principal investigator, after his death.
A rescue that did not work out

Swift has no thrusters of its own to fight drag, and strong solar activity in recent years puffed up the upper atmosphere and sped up its descent. NASA paid Katalyst Space Technologies about $30 million for a commercial spacecraft called LINK that would grab Swift and push it back up to a higher orbit. LINK launched on July 3, 2026, on a Northrop Grumman Pegasus XL rocket, but soon developed attitude-control problems and went into an unplanned spin. On August 19, NASA and Katalyst concluded the capture could not go ahead, as reported by SpacePolicyOnline and others. After Swift reached about 275 kilometers on October 20, the mission operations team at Penn State sent the commands that ended science work and prepared the spacecraft for reentry.

The mission is led from NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, where S. Bradley Cenko serves as principal investigator, with operations run by Penn State under operations director John Nousek. Shawn Domagal-Goldman, who directs NASA's Astrophysics Division, said the agency is looking at ways, including commercial and new missions, to keep a rapid-response capability for sudden cosmic events. Swift's archive, nearly 22 years of measurements and more than 1.5 million ultraviolet and optical images totaling about 12 terabytes, stays open to anyone.

Viraj's perspective: Swift is a reminder that the most valuable instrument is not always the biggest one, but the one that can react fastest. Losing it leaves a real gap for catching short-lived events like neutron star mergers. The thing I will watch is whether NASA follows through on a replacement for that fast-pointing role, and whether in-orbit servicing like Katalyst's attempt matures enough to save the next aging observatory.

title: Triple-Action Retatrutide Outperforms Ozempic in a Head-to-Head Diabetes Trial
dek: In an 80-week Phase 3 trial of 1,298 adults with type 2 diabetes, Eli Lilly's experimental drug retatrutide lowered blood sugar further than Ozempic's top dose and produced roughly twice the weight loss, according to topline results the company released on October 28.
body: On October 28, Eli Lilly and Company reported the first results from TRANSCEND-T2D-2, a Phase 3 trial that put its experimental medicine retatrutide directly against Novo Nordisk's Ozempic (semaglutide) at 2 mg, the highest dose approved for type 2 diabetes. It is the first late-stage study to compare retatrutide with another drug in this class rather than with a placebo. On both of the trial's main measures, blood sugar and body weight, retatrutide came out ahead.
Three hormone signals instead of one or two

Ozempic copies a single gut hormone, GLP-1, which helps the body release insulin and makes people feel full. Lilly's existing drug Mounjaro adds a second hormone signal called GIP. Retatrutide goes a step further: one weekly injection switches on receptors for GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. The idea is that adding glucagon's signal boosts energy use, pushing weight loss beyond what current drugs achieve.

The study enrolled 1,298 adults whose diabetes was not well controlled on metformin, some of whom also took an SGLT2 inhibitor. On average they started with an A1C, a measure of long-term blood sugar, of 8.3 percent and weighed about 102 kilograms (226 pounds). Participants were randomly assigned to retatrutide at 9 mg or 12 mg, or to Ozempic 2 mg, and were followed for 80 weeks.

Both retatrutide doses cut A1C by 2.2 percentage points, compared with 1.8 points for Ozempic. The trial's formal goal was to show the 12 mg dose was at least as good as Ozempic, and Lilly says it went further and proved statistically better. Weight loss was where the gap was widest: about 19.5 percent of body weight on 9 mg and 20.9 percent on 12 mg, versus 9.4 percent on Ozempic. Lilly also reported larger improvements in triglycerides, non-HDL cholesterol and systolic blood pressure.
Side effects and the fine print

Stomach-related problems were the most common side effects in every group. Diarrhea and vomiting were somewhat more frequent on the higher retatrutide dose, while constipation was less common on retatrutide than on Ozempic. More people stopped treatment because of side effects on retatrutide (4.8 percent on 9 mg and 7.9 percent on 12 mg) than on Ozempic (2.7 percent).

These are company-released topline numbers, not yet peer reviewed. The headline figures use an analysis that assumes everyone stayed on their assigned drug for the full 80 weeks, which typically yields larger effects than counting everyone who dropped out. The trial was also open-label, meaning participants and doctors knew which drug was being given. Retatrutide remains investigational and is not approved anywhere. Lilly, which ran the study, says full results will be presented at a medical meeting and published in a journal, and Kenneth Custer, who leads its cardiometabolic business, said the drug, if approved, "could shift the treatment paradigm" for type 2 diabetes. A separate Lilly trial, TRIUMPH-5, is now comparing retatrutide with the company's own tirzepatide.

Viraj's perspective: Placebo-controlled trials tell you a drug works; head-to-head trials tell you whether it is worth switching. Doubling Ozempic's weight loss while also beating it on blood sugar is a strong signal that adding a third hormone target pays off. What I will be watching is the peer-reviewed paper: how the results hold up when dropouts are counted, why more people quit on the higher dose, and whether the TRIUMPH-5 comparison against tirzepatide shows the same kind of gap. Tolerability, price and supply will decide how many patients actually benefit.

title: A Soft Robot That Crawls Like a Snake Could Reach the Gut's Hardest-to-Reach Stretch
dek: MIT engineers have built an inflatable, snake-inspired robotic enteroscope that grips and steers its way through the small intestine, and in animal tests it captured images, took tissue samples and sprayed fluid on target, according to a study in Science Robotics.
body: The small intestine is one of the hardest places in the body for doctors to reach. It is more than 20 feet long, only about an inch wide, and coiled tightly between the stomach and the colon. Standard endoscopes reach the ends, but examining the long middle usually requires a technique called double-balloon enteroscopy, which MIT describes as slow and laborious. A team led by Giovanni Traverso, a professor of mechanical engineering at MIT and a gastroenterologist at Brigham and Women's Hospital, has now built a soft robot designed to make that trip easier. Their study, published on October 28 in Science Robotics, describes the device and its first tests in animals.

Snakes steer by tightening muscles on one side of the body and then the other. The MIT robot copies that idea with soft, tube-shaped actuators that each contain four chambers. Inflating the chambers in different combinations lets the tube stretch forward or bend in any direction. To move along, the robot's head and tail carry balloons that take turns expanding and relaxing, so one end anchors against the intestinal wall while the other end pushes ahead, much like an inchworm.

Grip is the hard part on slippery, delicate tissue. The team wrapped the head and tail in sleeves cut with kirigami patterns, a paper-cutting technique the Traverso lab has used before for shoe soles and medical stents. The sleeves lie flat until a balloon stretches them, at which point tiny three-dimensional spikes pop up, a bit like a snake's scales catching the ground. The robot is tethered to an external controller, which MIT likens to a 3D-printed video game controller, and can enter through either the mouth or the rectum.

Down a hollow central channel, the robot carries tools: a camera, a sprayer for delivering drugs, and clips for taking biopsies or removing polyps. In animal studies the robot traveled about six and a half feet through the small intestine while the researchers demonstrated all three tools. Popular Science reports that the tests took place in sedated pigs, whose digestive anatomy is similar to ours, and that the robot captured live images, collected small tissue samples and delivered fluid to chosen spots. No human testing has been reported.
Who built it and what comes next

The paper's lead authors are Binbin Ying, a former MIT postdoc now an assistant professor at UT Southwestern Medical Center; Ahmad Mujtaba Jebran, an MIT graduate student; and Sahab Babaee, a former MIT research scientist. The team says it is now improving the robot's navigation and testing it for more tasks in the small intestine. Traverso's longer-term aim is more automated examination of the organ. "We hope we can continue to move it forward," he told MIT News.

Viraj's perspective: Soft robots often look clever in the lab and struggle in the body, so the meaningful detail here is the combination of passive grip and simple pneumatic steering that worked inside living tissue while carrying real clinical tools. The big questions now are speed, safety on inflamed or fragile intestines, and how much a physician still has to drive it by hand. Watch for human feasibility studies and side-by-side comparisons with double-balloon enteroscopy; those will decide whether this becomes a hospital tool or stays a striking demo.
